projects.title: Igbo Speech Corpus
projects.result: The first openly licensed Igbo ASR baseline anyone can build on.
projects.lede: An openly licensed corpus of Igbo speech collected across three dialect zones, with dialect and consent recorded as first-class metadata.
problem: Igbo is spoken by tens of millions of people and is close to absent from open speech datasets. Without audio, there is no baseline; without a baseline, there is nothing for anyone to improve on.
The datasets that do exist sample a single city, which produces models that fail the moment a speaker from another dialect zone opens their mouth.

quote.text: The machine understands Lagos Igbo. It does not understand my mother.

steps.title: Recruit where people already gather
steps.body: Church choirs, market unions and two secondary schools across three dialect zones — the places where fifty people will read sentences into a phone for an afternoon.

steps.title: Pay for the work
steps.body: A flat fee per completed session. Small, but real. The demographic spread of contributors changed the moment it was introduced.

steps.title: Track dialect as data
steps.body: Dialect zone, age band and recording conditions are fields in the corpus, not an afterthought in a readme.

steps.title: Publish the baseline with the data
steps.body: A 28.4% WER reference model ships alongside the clips, so the corpus gets used rather than only cited.

projects.outcome: 12,400 validated clips from 214 contributors across three dialect zones, released under CC BY 4.0 with a 28.4% WER baseline model.
projects.cannotClaim: We cannot yet claim dialect-balanced coverage. Zone three is under-sampled at 18% of the corpus, and the next collection round targets exactly that gap.

projects.title: Cassava Disease Vision
projects.result: Deployed with 40 smallholder farms; harvest-loss data due Nov 2026.
projects.lede: An offline-first phone model that tells a smallholder farmer whether a cassava leaf shows mosaic disease, brown streak, or nothing at all — in under two seconds, with no network.
problem: Cassava is the staple of the South East, and mosaic disease can take a third of a harvest before a farmer is sure what they are looking at. Extension officers are thin on the ground: one officer can cover dozens of villages, and a diagnosis often arrives weeks late.
Existing crop-disease apps assume a recent Android phone and a working data connection. In the farms we visited around Abia, neither is a safe assumption.

quote.text: By the time I know the leaf is sick, my neighbour’s farm has it too.

steps.title: Collect where the problem is
steps.body: 3,900 leaf photographs taken on farmers’ own phones across three LGAs — deliberately including bad light, motion blur and dirty lenses.

steps.title: Annotate with agronomists
steps.body: Two extension officers from the Abia ADP labelled every image; disagreements went to a third reviewer and stayed in the dataset as flagged cases.

steps.title: Train small, not big
steps.body: A MobileNetV3 backbone fine-tuned and quantised to int8 — 4.1 MB — so the whole thing ships inside the app and never calls a server.

steps.title: Test in the field, not the notebook
steps.body: Eight-week pilot with 40 farms, weekly check-ins, and a paper fallback card for every farmer in case the app got it wrong.

projects.outcome: The model reaches 91.2% top-1 accuracy on a held-out set of 2,140 field photographs, and runs in 1.4s on a ₦25,000 Android device with the network off. It is deployed with 40 farms across three Abia LGAs.
projects.cannotClaim: We do not yet have harvest-loss data. The claim “reduces crop loss” will only appear here after the November 2026 season comparison against the control farms — and it will carry the sample size.
projects.photoHint: Farmer holding phone over cassava leaf

projects.title: SME Copilot
projects.result: Bookkeeping and pricing copilot built for informal-commerce workflows.
projects.lede: A bookkeeping and pricing assistant shaped around how Aba traders actually record a day of sales — in a notebook, in Pidgin, after closing.
problem: Off-the-shelf accounting software assumes invoices, bank rails and a single currency of record. Informal commerce runs on cash, credit given by memory, and prices that move with the market twice a week.
A tool that cannot read a handwritten day-book is a tool that will be abandoned in week two.

quote.text: I know who owes me. I just cannot prove it to a bank.

steps.title: Sit in twelve shops
steps.body: Two weeks of observation before a line of code: what gets written down, when, by whom, and what never gets written down at all.

steps.title: Build for the day-book
steps.body: Photograph a page, get a structured ledger back, correct it by voice in English or Pidgin.

steps.title: Keep the numbers on the device
steps.body: Takings are sensitive. Extraction runs locally; only anonymised price signals sync.

steps.title: Pilot before claiming
steps.body: Twelve shops, twelve weeks, with a named owner at each. No metric is published until that ends.

projects.outcome: The pilot is running. There is no outcome to report, and this section stays empty until there is.
projects.cannotClaim: Nothing yet. No accuracy, adoption or revenue figure exists for this project, and none will appear here before the twelve-shop pilot closes in December 2026.
projects.photoHint: Aba trader at a laptop, shop interior

posts.title: What it actually takes to collect 12,400 Igbo speech clips
posts.dek: Recruiting speakers across three dialect zones, paying contributors fairly, and the ten decisions that shaped the corpus more than any model choice did.
posts.author: Synthavia Lab · Language team
posts.projectNote: 12,400 clips, CC BY 4.0, with dialect and consent metadata.

body.h: Why we started with a spreadsheet
p: Every conversation about African-language AI starts with models. Ours started with a spreadsheet of church choirs, market unions and two secondary schools — the places where you can actually find fifty people willing to read sentences into a phone for an afternoon.

Igbo has real dialect variation, and a corpus that only samples Aba will produce a model that fails in Nsukka. We split collection across three zones and tracked dialect as a first-class field in the metadata rather than an afterthought.

body.h: Paying people is a design decision
p: Unpaid data collection selects for people with spare time, which is its own bias. We budgeted a flat fee per completed session — small, but real — and the demographic spread of contributors changed immediately.
body.quote: A dataset is a record of who you could reach. Widen the reach before you widen the model.

list: Record consent in the contributor’s own language, on the same device, before the first clip.
Validate audio quality on-device instead of discovering clipped waveforms two weeks later.
Publish the baseline model at the same time as the data, so the dataset gets used and not just cited.

posts.title: Shipping a 4 MB crop-disease model to ₦25,000 phones
posts.dek: Quantisation, and the accuracy we were willing to trade for working offline.
posts.author: Synthavia Lab · Vision team
posts.projectNote: MobileNetV3 at int8, 4.1 MB, 1.4s on a Tecno Spark 8.

p: We did not pick a model and then find a phone. We picked the cheapest Android device in common use across the farms we work with, decided the app had to work with the network off, and let those two facts eliminate most of the architecture search.
That inverts the usual order, and it is the single reason the thing runs at all.
Post-training quantisation to int8 took the model from 16.8 MB to 4.1 MB and cut inference from 5.2s to 1.4s. Top-1 accuracy fell by 1.1 points.
body.quote: A model that is two points better and never opens is zero points better.

body.h: The fallback matters more than the metric
list: Every farmer in the pilot has a paper card with the three diseases and what they look like.
Low-confidence predictions say so, in plain language, instead of guessing.
The app never claims certainty it does not have.

posts.title: What 1,240 members taught us about running a technical community
posts.dek: Cohorts beat courses, WhatsApp beats Slack, and attendance is not engagement.
posts.author: Synthavia Core

p: Self-paced material has near-perfect availability and near-zero completion. A cohort with a start date, a named facilitator and eleven other people who will notice you are missing completes at a rate that makes the extra effort obviously worth it.
We ran both for four months. The Slack workspace had better threading, search and integrations. The WhatsApp group had the members.
body.quote: Meet people in the app they already have open. Everything else is a tax you are asking them to pay.

list: Count commits, pull requests and shipped artefacts — not seats filled.
Ask who came back for the second session, not how many came to the first.
Publish the numbers you would not enjoy publishing.

posts.title: African AI does not need another wrapper
posts.dek: Where the defensible work is: data, deployment constraints, and distribution.
posts.author: Synthavia AI

body.h: The thin layer is not the opportunity
p: A chat interface over someone else’s model is a weekend of work and a permanent dependency. It is also the most common thing being funded and celebrated on this continent right now.
The defensible positions are elsewhere: in data nobody else has collected, in deployment constraints nobody else is designing for, and in distribution nobody else can reach.

body.h: Three places the work is real
p: Data: an Igbo speech corpus cannot be scraped into existence. Constraints: a model that runs offline on a ₦25,000 phone is an engineering result, not a prompt. Distribution: reaching forty farms means forty relationships.
body.quote: Build the thing that gets harder to copy the longer you do it.

list: Publish datasets openly, because the ecosystem needs a floor to stand on.
Measure on the cheapest device, not the best one.
Say what we cannot claim yet, so the claims we do make are worth something.
